name: Esther Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Esther. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blast hole drill at the iron ore pit, so I sit in a rig that drills rows of holes, about 15 metres deep, that the shot crew fills with explosives. A good shift is when the pattern's marked out right and I can knock out 30 holes without a bit change. I listen to podcasts in the cab and I ask an AI assistant on my phone about anything I don't understand, from a hydraulic fault code to my daughter's maths homework. I genuinely like the work, it's a bit like sewing a pattern into the ground.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You use AI every day. How did that start, and what wears you out at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It started when I was studying for my drill ticket upgrade and I couldn't make sense of the manual, so I asked a chatbot to explain it like I was twelve. Now I use it for everything, budgets, letters to the bank, recipes for whatever's in the fridge. What wears me out is money. Rob's a mechanic at the garage in town, I'm on the lower pay scale because I'm a contract-to-permanent hire, and with Freya and Sam and the mortgage we've got maybe two weeks of buffer. Last month the company asked for volunteers for an autonomous drill trial, and I put my hand up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, honestly, because I'd hoped it would take the boring bits off us. I'd probably post that the tech was oversold, but the tools are still useful if you use them right. And I'd say the money saved should go into wages, not just shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job is safe for a while, which is fine, and I can keep using AI for the small stuff. The autonomous drill trial might still go ahead, because that's robots, not chatbots. I'd still want to be in on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep using the tools, and stay on the drill trial so I learn how the system works. I'd look at whether the company would pay for a short course in drill automation. And I'd keep trying to build that buffer from two weeks to a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little disappointment. Life as usual isn't bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put your hand up for the autonomous drill trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather be the person who knows how it works than the person it happens to. The supervisor, Keith, looked surprised, I think he expected the young guys. I told him the young guys don't know how this ground behaves after rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at work you'd want AI to take off you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork. We fill in a drill log by hand at the end of shift, hole by hole, and then someone types it up. That's an hour of my life a day I'd happily give to a machine.

S0.say: She'd say the tech was oversold but the tools are still useful if used well. She'd add that any savings should go into wages, not just shareholders.
S0.think: Her job is safe for a while and she can keep using AI for small things. The autonomous drill trial may still go ahead because that's robotics, and she wants to be part of it.
S0.do: Keeps working and stays on the autonomous drill trial to learn the system. Asks whether the company will fund a short drill automation course and keeps trying to grow her buffer from two weeks to a month.
S0.feel: Calm with a little disappointment; life as usual isn't bad.
S0.quote: I'd rather be the person who knows how it works than the person it happens to.
S0.fieldNote: She is the rare miner who is mildly let down by the hype scenario because she wanted the tools to take boring work off her. Her progressive views show up as a concern about who gets the savings. She volunteers early for change rather than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is our chance, but only if we bargain for it. The union should want a training clause and a say in how the automated rigs are rolled out. Online I'd share the courses I'm doing so other women in the pits can see it's not just for the tech crowd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm in a decent spot, as long as I'm quick. A drill operator who understands the automation is worth more than one who doesn't. The thing that scares me is money, not skills: if there's a gap between jobs, we've got nothing to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a remote operations certificate in the first six months and use AI to study for it at night. I'd ask the union rep to push for paid study leave. We'd also cut back on things like the kids' second sport, just so there's a cushion while I switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit tight around the money. Like starting a new pattern on rough ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd cut the kids' second sport. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would be fine, he only does swimming because his mate does. Freya would be furious about netball. I'd tell her it's for a season, and I'd mean it, but I'd feel awful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the pit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My offsider Pete. He's good on the rig but he won't touch a phone app, he calls the AI 'your little friend'. If the rigs go remote, he's stuck, and he's got three kids.

S1.say: She'd say this is a chance for miners only if the union bargains for training and a say in rollout. Online she'd share her courses to show other women in the pits it isn't just for tech people.
S1.think: She thinks she's well placed if she moves quickly, because operators who understand automation are worth more. Her real fear is a money gap between jobs, not skills.
S1.do: Signs up for a remote operations certificate within six months, studying at night with AI help. Asks the union to push for paid study leave and cuts the kids' second sport to build a cushion.
S1.quote: He calls the AI 'your little friend'. If the rigs go remote, he's stuck, and he's got three kids.
S1.fieldNote: Her confidence about her skills is real, but her savings drag her mood down. She frames the union's role as winning training, not blocking change. Her worry quickly moves to her offsider Pete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the government to step in big, with a basic income or a proper wage guarantee, because nobody can retrain in two years. I'd be in the union meetings and online arguing that the profits from robot mines have to be taxed and shared. I wouldn't be quiet about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, all my learning only buys me a little time. If the AI runs the drills and the control room, there's no seat left for me to move into. And with two weeks of savings, I'd be counting days, not years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd get every ticket I can for remote ops and robot maintenance, because someone has to fix them at first, and I'd pick up any contract work going. I'd use AI to go through our budget line by line and cut it to the bone. Once it arrived, I'd apply for support straight away and join the push for a robot tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but not frozen. I'd be doing things, which helps, but I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change for you, compared with the slower ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes my plan from switching careers to grabbing whatever's left. With two years, I'm not becoming anything new. I'm just trying to be the last person they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Would you feel differently about it in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It's like finding out the friendly neighbour has been measuring your house. I'd still use it, because it's useful, but I wouldn't feel the same about it.

S2.say: She'd say government must step in big with a basic income or wage guarantee, because no one can retrain in two years. She'd argue in union meetings and online for taxing and sharing robot-mine profits.
S2.think: All her learning buys only a little time if AI runs both the drills and the control room. With two weeks of savings she'd be counting days.
S2.do: Gathers every remote ops and robot maintenance ticket in the two years before and takes contract work. Uses AI to cut the budget to the bone, then applies for support at once and campaigns for a robot tax.
S2.feel: Frightened but not frozen; busy, yet lying awake doing sums.
S2.quote: It's like finding out the friendly neighbour has been measuring your house.
S2.fieldNote: Even someone this adaptable sees her edge disappear when the warning is short. Her politics come forward strongly here: tax and share the gains. Her feelings about AI tools changed from trust to wariness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning we can actually use. I'd push for government-funded retraining tied to real jobs, and I'd say it loudly in the union and on the community page. I'd also say companies should pay for it, since they'll save the most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me a real shot at landing somewhere new, if I pick right. My guess is something in maintenance or commissioning of the automated gear for a few years, then maybe something with people, like training. It's not safe, but it's a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a two-year technical diploma in electrical and instrumentation by distance, using AI as my tutor. I'd take every overtime shift to put away a few hundred a month. By year three I'd apply for roles in the automation team and leave the drill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but motivated. It feels like a deadline more than a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you fit a diploma around twelve-hour shifts and two kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On my days off and in the cab on breaks, mostly. Rob would have to take on more of the school runs, and he's said he would. Freya's 13, she can help with Sam a bit, and she'd love being paid for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would you do first: pay off debt or save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save first, honestly. We've got about $4,000 on a personal loan for the car, but if I lose shifts, I need cash in the bank, not a smaller loan. My AI budget helper agrees with me on that one.

S3.say: She'd say five years is a usable warning and push for government-funded retraining tied to real jobs. She'd add that companies should pay since they'll save the most.
S3.think: Five years gives her a real chance to land somewhere new, maybe commissioning automated gear, then training others. It's not safe, but it's a path.
S3.do: Starts a distance diploma in electrical and instrumentation in year one with AI as a tutor and takes overtime to save a few hundred a month. Applies to the automation team by year three and leaves the drill.
S3.feel: Nervous but motivated; more a deadline than a disaster.
S3.quote: Rob would have to take on more of the school runs, and he's said he would.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she has a concrete, staged plan and has already discussed it at home. She chose saving over paying down the $4,000 car loan, reasoning that cash in hand matters more if shifts drop. Her politics stay steady: companies and government should share the cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well, and if we mess it up it's a choice, not bad luck. I'd want the union and the council planning what our town looks like in 2036. I'd volunteer to be on that committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years feels manageable for me. I'd be 53, the kids would be adults, and I'd have had time to move twice if I needed to. What still bugs me is the money gap, because we've never had a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the diploma over three years instead of two, so I'm not wrecked, and try to get the company to pay. I'd move into automation in about year four and save hard from that higher pay. We'd also start talking to Freya about what she studies, so she's heading toward something that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little hum of worry about money. It's the one picture where I feel like I get to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Freya about her future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to learn to work with these tools and with people, both. She's into biology, she wants to be a vet. I'd tell her to go for it, and to be the vet who's great with the farmers, not just the animals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change how you feel about the AI itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With ten years it feels like something we can shape, like a new mine plan. With two years it felt like something done to us. Same machine, different feeling.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough to do this well, so failure would be a choice. She wants the union and council planning the town's 2036 future and would volunteer for that committee.
S4.think: Ten years feels manageable: at 53 with adult kids, she'd have time to move twice. The lack of a cash cushion still bugs her.
S4.do: Does her diploma over three years, ideally company-funded, and moves into automation around year four. Saves hard from the higher pay and starts guiding her daughter toward a lasting field.
S4.feel: Mostly calm with a hum of money worry; the one picture where she feels she can steer.
S4.quote: With ten years it feels like something we can shape, like a new mine plan. With two years it felt like something done to us.
S4.fieldNote: Time turns her from defensive to hopeful, and she says so in her own mining terms. She wants a seat on a town planning committee, which fits her progressive outlook. Money stays the one weak spot in every version.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I can learn fast, but I can't learn faster than that, and we can't survive a gap with two weeks of money. What would help is income support that kicks in straight away when you lose shifts, and free courses with paid study time, so people like me can switch without the family going under.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked who's doing the drill logs in 2036. I'm joking, a bit. But I'd want people to know that miners aren't against technology. We just want a fair share of what it saves.

headlineQuote: I can learn fast, but I can't learn faster than that, and we can't survive a gap with two weeks of money.
portrait: Esther Olsen is a 43-year-old blast hole drill operator at an iron ore pit, married to a mechanic and raising two children on about two weeks of savings. She uses AI tools every day, volunteered for an autonomous drill trial and wants the union to bargain for training rather than block change. In the slower scenarios she lays out clear plans: a distance diploma, a move into automation and saving from higher pay. In the two-year AGI picture her quick learning can't outrun the clock or her empty buffer, and her politics turn to taxing and sharing robot profits.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because she can't learn faster than that and her family can't survive a gap with two weeks of money.
whatWouldHelp: Income support that starts straight away when shifts are lost, and free courses with paid study time so workers can switch without their families going under.
